summary.text: Newton’s second law put to work on problems with more than one step: two blocks joined by a string (the system’s acceleration first, then the tension from one block), scale readings in an elevator and working back from a reading, a pull at an angle, friction worked out from a measured slide down a ramp, and reading a force–acceleration graph whose slope is 1 ÷ the mass.

why.text: Real problems rarely hand you the net force. Breaking one into a system step and an object step, or into a vertical and a horizontal step, is the move every later unit — friction, circular motion, energy — builds on.

objectives.text: Use a free-body diagram and ΣF = ma to find an acceleration.
Find the acceleration of connected objects and the tension between them.
Find a scale reading in an accelerating elevator, and the acceleration from a reading.
Find the normal force and acceleration for a pull at an angle.
Interpret the slope of an acceleration–force graph as 1 ÷ mass.
Follow a fixed order of steps for multi-object problems.

parentNote.text: From N2L_Worksheet.pdf in the new Dynamics 2 folder. The sheet was read for what it asks — connected blocks and tension, elevator scale readings, an angled pull with friction, a block on a ramp, and a force–acceleration data table — and nothing of hers was marked or recorded. Dynamics 1 already teaches the second law, tension, apparent weight and slopes in words, so this unit is the multi-step layer: the system’s acceleration first, then the tension from one block; a scale reading forward and backward; the normal force before anything that depends on it. Every number was computed with sympy and checked, every wrong option is a named slip (one block’s mass only, tension equal to the pull, the sign of a flipped, a speed used as an acceleration, sine and cosine swapped, friction added), and none of the sheet’s numbers is reused. This unit uses g = 9.8 m/s²; her sheets may write it as −9.8 or 10, and a card says so. One thing on the sheet: free-response problem 3 skips part (d), going straight from (c) to (e).

nextUp.text: Read the cards, then take the quiz. Before every calculation, draw the arrows and say which way is positive.

cards.def:
**Draw the forces, pick a positive direction, add the forces along it, and set the total equal to ma.**
• One free-body diagram per object, with every force on THAT object.
• Forces along your positive direction are +, against it are −.
• Only then put numbers in. Most wrong answers start as a missing or backwards arrow.

**This unit uses g = 9.8 m/s² as a size, and says “down” in words.**
• Your sheets may write g = −9.8 m/s², or round it to 10. The minus is only the direction: down.
• A weight is mg using the size of g. If your class uses 10, your answers will be about 2 percent bigger than these, and both are right for their g.
cards.hint: The minus sign on g means “down”, nothing more.

cards.def:
**Two objects joined by a taut string move together, so they have the same acceleration.**
• If one sped up more, the string would go slack or snap.
• So treat them as ONE system first: the outside force over the total mass.

cards.term: The string is internal to the system
cards.def:
**When both blocks are one system, the string’s pulls cancel and drop out.**
• The string pulls the front block back and the back block forward by the same amount.
• That is why the system equation has no T in it — and why you need a second step to find T.

cards.term: Then the tension from one block
cards.def:
**To find the tension, write ΣF = ma for ONE block, using only the forces on it.**
• The easiest block is the one the string pulls and nothing else does: T = m_that block × a.
• You already know a from the system step.

cards.term: The tension is less than the pull
cards.def:
**The pull speeds up both blocks; the string only has to speed up the one behind it, so the tension is smaller than the pull.**
• Setting the tension equal to the applied force is the commonest slip.
• The tension is the pull’s share for the trailing block: T = F × m_back / (m₁ + m₂).
cards.hint: The string only drags what is behind it.

cards.def:
**Pull the other block with the same force and the acceleration stays the same, but the tension changes.**
• The total mass is unchanged, so a is unchanged.
• Now the string drags the OTHER block, so T = that block’s mass × a. Pulling the lighter block gives the bigger tension.

cards.term: Scale reading: speeding up going up
cards.def:
**When the acceleration points up, the scale reads more than your weight: N = m(g + a).**
• The floor has to hold you up AND push you faster.
• Speeding up on the way up and slowing down on the way down both have an upward acceleration.

**When the acceleration points down, the scale reads less: N = m(g − a).**
• Slowing down on the way UP is an acceleration down — the reading drops even though you are rising.
• Flipping the sign of a is the slip to watch for: decide the direction of the acceleration, not the direction of travel.

**At constant velocity the scale reads exactly your weight, however fast the elevator moves.**
• Constant velocity means a = 0, so N = mg.
• A speed is not an acceleration: 4 m/s up adds nothing to the reading.

cards.term: From a scale reading back to the acceleration
cards.def:
**Divide the reading by the mass and subtract g; what is left is the acceleration.**
• A positive answer points up, a negative one points down.
• Forgetting to subtract g gives an absurd acceleration — a quick check that something went wrong.

cards.term: An angled pull lifts as well as drags
cards.def:
**The vertical part of an upward pull, F sin θ, takes some of the weight, so the normal force shrinks.**
• N = mg − F sin θ on a level floor.
• Only the horizontal part, F cos θ, speeds the object along the floor.
• Less normal force means less friction, which is the next unit’s story.

**On a frictionless floor, a steeper pull always gives a smaller acceleration, because cos θ shrinks.**
• On a rough floor it is a trade: less horizontal drive, but less friction too. Tilting a little can help; tilting a lot never does.

cards.term: Working back to friction on a slope
cards.def:
**If you measure how fast something slides down a slope, the shortfall from g sin θ is friction’s doing.**
• Down the slope: mg sin θ − f = ma, so f = mg sin θ − ma.
• On a frictionless slope a would be g sin θ; anything less is friction.

cards.term: Acceleration against force: a straight line
cards.def:
**For one cart of fixed mass, acceleration is proportional to the net force, so a graph of a against F is a straight line through the origin.**
• Double the force, double the acceleration.

**The slope of a against F is 1 ÷ the mass, in (m/s²) per newton, which is 1/kg.**
• a = (1/m) F has the same shape as y = mx.
• So the mass is 1 ÷ slope: a steeper line means a lighter cart.

cards.term: Which variable goes on which axis
cards.def:
**The one you choose goes across the bottom; the one you measure goes up the side.**
• Choosing the force and measuring the acceleration makes force the independent variable and acceleration the dependent one.

cards.term: Acceleration follows the net force, not the motion
cards.def:
**The acceleration always points the way the net force points — even when the object is moving the other way.**
• A box sliding left while slowing down has a net force to the right.
• Velocity tells you where it is going; acceleration tells you how that is changing.

questions.q: Two blocks on a frictionless table are joined by a taut string, and one block is pulled so both speed up. How do their accelerations compare?
opts: They are equal, because the taut string makes them move together
The pulled block’s is bigger, because the force acts on it directly
The heavier block’s is smaller, because it has more inertia to overcome
The block behind has none until the string stretches tight enough
questions.hint: What would happen to the string if one went faster?
steps: The string is taut and does not stretch.
If one block sped up more, the gap would change and the string would go slack.
So they keep the same velocity at every moment.
Same velocity at every moment means the same acceleration.

ex.main: **A taut string forces the two blocks to share one acceleration.** The pulled block feels a bigger net force, but it is not ahead: the string holds the gap fixed. That is what makes the one-system step work.
ex.tip: Joined and taut means one acceleration.

questions.q: A 3.0 kg block and a 5.0 kg block sit on a frictionless table, joined by a light string. A 40 N horizontal pull acts on the 5.0 kg block. What is the acceleration of the blocks?
questions.hint: Both blocks move, so both masses count.
steps: The string makes the blocks one system.

ex.main: **a = 40 N ÷ (3.0 + 5.0) kg = 5.0 m/s².** 8.0 m/s² uses only the pulled block’s mass, 13 m/s² only the other block’s, and 20 m/s² subtracts the masses — but the pull has to speed up everything joined to it.
ex.tip: System first: outside force over total mass.

questions.q: A 3.0 kg block and a 5.0 kg block sit on a frictionless table, joined by a light string. A 40 N horizontal pull acts on the 5.0 kg block, so both accelerate at 5.0 m/s². What is the tension in the string?
questions.hint: Which block does the string pull, and nothing else?
steps: The string is the only horizontal force on the 3.0 kg block.

ex.main: **T = 3.0 kg × 5.0 m/s² = 15 N.** 40 N sets the tension equal to the pull; 25 N uses the pulled block’s mass, which the string does not drag; 20 N splits the pull evenly, as if the blocks had equal masses.
ex.tip: Find T from the block the string drags.

questions.q: A 3.0 kg block and a 5.0 kg block sit on a frictionless table, joined by a light string. A 40 N horizontal pull now acts on the 3.0 kg block instead, pulling the other way. What are the acceleration and the tension?
questions.hint: The total mass has not changed. The block being dragged has.
steps: The system is still 8.0 kg, so a = 40 N ÷ 8.0 kg = 5.0 m/s².
Now the string drags the 5.0 kg block.
The answer is 5.0 m/s² and 25 N.

ex.main: **Same acceleration, 5.0 m/s², but the tension rises to 25 N.** The string now drags the heavier block. Carrying 15 N over ignores which block is behind; 40 N sets the tension equal to the pull; 13 m/s² counts only the pulled block’s mass.
ex.tip: Pull the lighter block and the string works harder.

questions.q: Two crates joined by a rope are pulled across smooth ice by a second rope on the front crate. Why is the tension in the joining rope less than the pull on the front rope?
opts: The joining rope only speeds up the back crate; the pull speeds up both
Some of the pull is used up stretching the joining rope as they move
Tension always shrinks along a rope, so the far end pulls less hard
The back crate pushes forward on the front crate and cancels some pull
questions.hint: How much mass does each rope have to accelerate?
steps: Both crates share the same acceleration.
The front rope must give that acceleration to both crates.
The joining rope must give it only to the back crate.
Less mass at the same acceleration needs less force, so the tension is smaller.

ex.main: **The front rope accelerates both crates; the joining rope accelerates only the back one**, so it needs less force. A light rope passes its tension along unchanged, and the back crate pulls back on the front one rather than pushing it forward.
ex.tip: Tension = the share of the pull for whatever is behind.

questions.q: A 56 kg student stands on a scale in an elevator that is speeding up as it rises, at 1.2 m/s². What does the scale read?
questions.hint: The acceleration points up, so the floor pushes harder than her weight.
steps: Upward is positive: N − mg = ma.

ex.main: **N = 56 × (9.8 + 1.2) = 616 N.** 482 N flips the sign of a; 549 N is her weight, ignoring the acceleration; 67 N is only ma, forgetting that the floor holds her up as well.
ex.tip: Upward acceleration: g + a.

questions.q: A 70 kg passenger stands on a scale in an elevator that is moving UP but slowing down at 2.5 m/s². What does the scale read?
questions.hint: Slowing while rising: which way does the acceleration point?
steps: Moving up and slowing down means the acceleration points down.
With up as positive, a = −2.5 m/s², so N = m(g − 2.5).

ex.main: **The acceleration points down, so N = 70 × (9.8 − 2.5) = 511 N.** 861 N uses g + a because the elevator is rising — the slip of reading the direction of travel instead of the acceleration. 686 N ignores the acceleration; 175 N is only ma.
ex.tip: Slowing on the way up feels light.

questions.q: A 58 kg student stands on a scale in an elevator rising at a steady 4.0 m/s. What does the scale read?
questions.hint: What is the acceleration at a steady speed?
steps: A steady speed in a straight line means a = 0.

ex.main: **Constant velocity means no acceleration, so N = mg = 568 N.** 800 N and 336 N treat the speed 4.0 m/s as if it were an acceleration; 58 N uses the mass as if it were a weight.
ex.tip: A speed is not an acceleration.

questions.q: A 45 kg student stands on a scale in a moving elevator, and the scale reads 504 N. What is the elevator’s acceleration?
questions.hint: Divide by the mass, then take g away.
steps: Upward is positive: N − mg = ma, so a = N / m − g.

ex.main: **a = 504 ÷ 45 − 9.8 = +1.4 m/s², upward** — the reading is above her weight (441 N), so the floor pushes her up harder than gravity pulls down. “Downward” flips the sign; 11.2 forgets to subtract g; 21.0 adds it.
ex.tip: Reading above the weight means acceleration up.

questions.q: A scale in an elevator reads LESS than the weight of the person standing on it. Which could the elevator be doing?
opts: Moving up at a steady speed
questions.hint: A low reading needs a downward acceleration.
steps: N < mg means the net force on the person points down.
Rising while slowing is an acceleration down; so is falling while speeding up.
Of the choices, only moving up and slowing down fits.

ex.main: **A low reading means the acceleration points down, and rising-but-slowing is exactly that.** A steady speed reads the weight; speeding up on the way up and slowing down on the way down both read MORE than the weight.
ex.tip: Ask which way the speed is changing, not which way it moves.

questions.q: A 15 kg crate on a level floor is pulled with 80 N by a rope angled 25° above the horizontal. What is the normal force from the floor?
questions.hint: The rope lifts a little as well as dragging.
steps: The rope’s vertical part: 80 sin 25° = 33.8 N, up.

ex.main: **N = mg − F sin θ = 147 − 33.8 ≈ 113 N.** 147 N leaves the rope’s lift out; 181 N adds it as if the rope pressed down; 74 N subtracts F cos θ — sine and cosine swapped.
ex.tip: Vertical part: sine, when the angle is from the horizontal.

questions.q: A 15 kg crate on a level floor is pulled with 80 N by a rope angled 25° above the horizontal, and kinetic friction on it is 40 N. What is its acceleration along the floor?
questions.hint: Only the horizontal part of the pull drives it along.
steps: Horizontal part of the pull: 80 cos 25° = 72.5 N.
Friction points backward: net force = 72.5 − 40 = 32.5 N.

ex.main: **a = (80 cos 25° − 40) ÷ 15 ≈ 2.2 m/s².** 2.7 uses the whole 80 N as if the rope were level; 7.5 adds friction instead of subtracting it; 4.8 leaves friction out.
ex.tip: Horizontal part forward, friction back.

questions.q: A cart on a frictionless floor is pulled by a rope with a force of fixed size. If the rope is tilted further above the horizontal, what happens to the cart’s acceleration?
opts: It decreases, because the horizontal part F cos θ gets smaller
It increases, because the normal force gets smaller
It stays the same, because the size of the pull has not changed
It increases, because the rope now lifts part of the cart’s weight
questions.hint: With no friction, only one part of the pull matters.
steps: Only the horizontal part, F cos θ, accelerates the cart along the floor.
As θ grows, cos θ shrinks.
There is no friction for a smaller normal force to reduce.

ex.main: **On a frictionless floor the acceleration falls as the rope tilts up**, because F cos θ shrinks. A smaller normal force only helps when there is friction to reduce; here there is none.
ex.tip: No friction: steeper pull, less acceleration.

questions.q: A 4.5 kg block slides down a 40° ramp, and its acceleration is measured as 4.1 m/s². How big is the friction on it?
questions.hint: Gravity’s part down the slope, minus what the acceleration needs.
steps: Down the slope: mg sin θ − f = ma.

ex.main: **f = mg sin θ − ma ≈ 28.3 − 18.5 = 9.9 N.** 47 N adds ma instead of subtracting it; 15 N uses cos 40° for the down-slope part, swapping sine and cosine; 28 N is gravity’s part alone, ignoring the acceleration.
ex.tip: Friction is the shortfall from g sin θ.

questions.q: The graph shown plots a cart’s acceleration against the net force on it, with the cart’s mass kept the same. What does the slope of the line stand for?
opts: The net force on the cart
questions.hint: Compare a = (1/m)F with y = mx.
steps: The line has the form a = (something) × F.
Newton’s second law gives a = F / m = (1/m) F.
So the slope is the number multiplying F.

ex.main: **The slope of a against F is 1/m.** Plotting F against a instead would make the slope the mass — which axis holds which quantity decides it.
ex.tip: Rise over run: (m/s²) per N is 1/kg.

questions.q: The graph shown plots a cart’s acceleration against the net force on it, with the cart’s mass kept the same. What is the cart’s mass?
questions.hint: Find the slope, then turn it upside down.

ex.main: **Slope 0.80 = 1/m, so m = 1.25 kg.** 0.80 kg reads the slope itself as the mass; 2.0 kg and 1.6 kg are just the largest force and the largest acceleration on the graph.
ex.tip: Steeper line, lighter cart.

questions.q: A cart of fixed mass speeds up at 0.80 m/s² for every newton of net force, along a straight line through the origin. What acceleration would a 3.5 N net force give it?
questions.hint: Multiply the force by the slope.

ex.main: **a = 0.80 × 3.5 = 2.8 m/s².** 4.4 divides by the slope instead of multiplying; 3.5 assumes a equals F; 1.6 assumes the line stops rising once the data run out.
ex.tip: A straight line through the origin keeps going.

questions.q: In an experiment, you choose the net force on a cart and measure the acceleration it gets. Which is the independent variable?
questions.hint: Which one do you set yourself?
steps: The independent variable is the one you choose and change.
The dependent variable is the one you measure.
Here you choose the force and measure the acceleration.

ex.main: **You set the net force, so it is the independent variable**, and it goes across the horizontal axis. The acceleration is what you measure; the mass is held constant, a controlled variable.
ex.tip: Choose it: independent. Measure it: dependent.

questions.q: A box slides to the left across a floor and is slowing down. Which way does the net force on it point?
questions.hint: Slowing down means the acceleration opposes the velocity.
steps: It is slowing, so its acceleration points opposite to its velocity: right.
The net force points the same way as the acceleration.

ex.main: **Right — the net force points along the acceleration, not along the motion.** Something moving left with a leftward net force would be speeding up, and zero net force would keep its speed constant.
ex.tip: Net force follows the acceleration.

questions.q: Put the steps for finding the tension between two connected blocks in order.
opts: Draw a free-body diagram for each block and pick a positive direction
Treat both blocks as one system and find a = F_net ÷ (m₁ + m₂)
Choose one block and write ΣF = ma using only the forces on it
Solve that one block’s equation for the tension T
questions.hint: You need the acceleration before the tension.
steps: Start with the forces: one diagram per block.
The system step gives a, because T cancels inside the system.
Then one block’s own equation contains T.

ex.main: **Diagrams, then the system’s acceleration, then one block’s equation, then T.** Trying to find T first fails: each block’s equation has two unknowns, T and a, until the system step supplies a.
ex.tip: System for a, one block for T.
